title: India's Inflation Just Crossed the RBI's Red Line. Fuel and Vegetables Did the Damage.
excerpt: Consumer prices likely rose 4% in May — breaching the central bank's target for the first time in 15 months — as four fuel price hikes and a punishing heatwave pushed transport and food costs sharply higher.
body:
India's consumer price inflation likely crossed the Reserve Bank of India's 4 per cent medium-term target in May for the first time in over a year, driven by rising vegetable prices and fuel costs that are now filtering through to transport and household budgets, according to a Reuters poll of 38 economists.

The consensus forecast puts May CPI inflation at 4.0 per cent, up from 3.48 per cent in April. If confirmed when official data is released later this week, it would mark the end of 15 consecutive months in which inflation remained below the RBI's target — a streak that had given the central bank room to focus on growth and currency defence rather than price stability.

The two forces pushing inflation higher are both consequences of the U.S.-Israeli war on Iran. First, fuel: state-owned oil marketing companies raised domestic fuel prices four times in May alone, pushing transport costs sharply higher. Transport inflation is estimated to have jumped to 4.15 per cent in May from near zero in April, contributing 36 basis points to headline inflation — up from effectively nothing a month earlier.

Second, food: a severe heatwave across northern and central India in May disrupted vegetable supply chains, sending tomato, onion, and green vegetable prices sharply higher in mandis across the country. Vegetable prices, which had been benign for most of the past year, rebounded with force.

"May '26 CPI likely crossed the 4 per cent threshold, driven primarily by vegetables and transport inflation," said Kanika Pasricha, chief economic adviser at Union Bank of India. "Persistence of elevated temperatures across several regions and war-led constraints have adversely impacted the supply of commodities."

## The RBI's Dilemma

The timing is particularly uncomfortable for the RBI, which chose to hold interest rates steady at its policy meeting last week. Governor Sanjay Malhotra said underlying inflation pressures remained "benign" and that the central bank was watching for second-round effects — the point at which higher fuel and food costs start feeding into wages, rents, and services prices.

But the decision not to hike rates was also strategic. The RBI wanted to focus on its $50 billion foreign exchange defence package — a suite of measures to attract NRI deposits and support the rupee — without muddying the message with a simultaneous rate increase. As economists at HSBC noted: "We believe the RBI did not want markets to get an impression that it wants to use rate defence for shoring up the INR."

That calculation now faces a test. If inflation stays above 4 per cent through June and July — which is likely, given that the monsoon is forecast below normal for the first time since 2023 and fuel prices show no sign of retreating — the pressure to raise rates will build.

## What This Means for Indian Households

For consumers, the squeeze is already visible. Indian companies from Hindustan Unilever to Dabur to Maruti Suzuki have rolled out price hikes across categories. Where price increases are not possible — particularly in mass-market segments where packs are anchored at ₹10 or ₹20 price points — companies are shrinking product sizes instead.

"We are reducing grammage because we can't breach those price points," Mohit Malhotra, global CEO of Dabur, told Reuters.

Airlines IndiGo and Air India are trimming capacity on fuel-heavy international routes and raising fares. Auto companies have passed through increases. And the latest LPG price hike — ₹29 per cylinder, effective June 7 — adds to the pressure on household budgets already stretched by a year of incremental cost increases.

For the Indian diaspora, the inflation number matters because it directly affects family purchasing power back home. The weaker rupee has made remittances more valuable in nominal terms, but rising prices are eroding that advantage in real terms. The next few months will determine whether this is a temporary spike driven by seasonal heat and war-related fuel costs, or the beginning of a more persistent inflationary cycle that forces the RBI's hand on rates.
